title: Overhauling My Word of the Day Routine 2026
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: A veteran first-grade teacher, writing for the Science of Reading Classroom blog, reflects on a daily "Word of the Day" routine she ran for years without questioning its impact. Students put a sight word into a sentence on a whiteboard, but she came to see that many of them had no real idea what a sentence is and would write fragments such as "went to the park" and believe they were finished. Training in Releasing Writers and reading The Writing Revolution alongside the Syntax Project slides convinced her that sentence-level instruction must be explicit and sequenced, and that her core ELA program supplied too little of it. She now starts from the basics, who or what the sentence is about and what is happening, then moves to sentence versus fragment, then expanding with when and where details. The routine is still the first thing students see at the door, but it now builds sentences using a gist format and has students notice what is missing and fix it themselves.
points: A long-standing routine can persist unexamined; the useful question is what it actually teaches.
Many young writers do not know what a sentence is, so assuming they absorb structure from reading and talking leaves some children behind.
Explicit, sequenced instruction beginning at the word and sentence level, drawn from The Writing Revolution, fills the gap that a core program leaves.
Mastering one step at a time (subject, predicate, fragment, expansion) produces self-correction, such as noticing the missing "who".
The same routine can change purpose when it is rebuilt around structure instead of sight-word recall.
quotes: My students are bright and curious, but they did not have any sense of what a sentence actually is. When I asked them to write, they had wonderful ideas, but their ideas came out onto the paper as fragments, or even strings of words that had no clear focus and did not hold together.
A child might write “went to the park,” and they truly believed they had finished a sentence. No one had ever shown them what makes a sentence a sentence.

I realized I had been assuming that children would grasp sentence structure naturally through reading, listening, and talking. I can say that for some of my children that happens, but for many it does not.
It was the first time I began to reflect on my writing instruction and understand the importance of starting at the word and sentence level with our youngest writers.
If we expect students to meet these expectations, they need far more explicit, sustained instruction than the program provides on its own.

Moving step by step has allowed my first graders to master each skill before adding on the next, and it has given me a clearer picture of what explicit sentence level instruction looks like in practice.
A child who once wrote “went to the park” will now pause, notice that the “who” is missing, and fix it on their own.

The routine I once did without a second thought has become a daily opportunity for students to think about sentences, talk about them, and take ownership of their writing. Same routine, but now it has a purpose.
